title: Hermits and consecrated virgins

lines: A PHARMACIST WITH A PLAIN RING.
A CABIN, A VOW, A SILENCE.
cards: A hospital pharmacist finishes her shift, takes the bus home to a small apartment, and prays the Church's evening prayer at her kitchen table. On her right hand is a plain ring.
Years ago, in her cathedral, the bishop consecrated her to Christ, and she went back to work the next morning. A few hours' drive away, a man lives alone in a cabin on land his diocese lent him.
He has made vows into the hands of his bishop. He grows vegetables, keeps silence, and prays through the night for a world that mostly doesn't know he's there. Neither belongs to an order.
Both callings reach back to the early Church.

teach.b: Back on day two hundred eighty-two, a monk moved into a small house in the woods.
The prophet Elijah, worn out and running for his life, goes into the desert and on to the mountain of God, and the Lord isn't in the wind, or the earthquake, or the fire.

teach.h: A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "and after the fire a whistling of a gentle air." Hermits go looking for that whisper.
In the early centuries, tradition says, men and women went into the Egyptian desert to pray alone; the Life of Antony tells of one.

teach.h: A VIRGIN CONSECRATED IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: The Catechism describes hermits today: giving their lives to the praise of God and the salvation of the world through a stricter separation from the world, the silence of solitude, and constant prayer and penance.
Church law recognizes a hermit who professes the evangelical counsels publicly in the hands of the diocesan bishop and lives under his guidance. Now the consecrated virgin.
The Catechism says that from apostolic times, Christian virgins, called by the Lord, gave themselves to him with an undivided heart.
The Church keeps a rite for it today: a woman who has never married is consecrated by her bishop in a solemn liturgy, joined to Christ as a bride.

teach.h: AFTER THE FIRE, A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.
teach.b: She may live in a community, or in the world, at her own job, in her own apartment, under the bishop's care.
The Catechism calls the hermit's life a reminder of the inward side of the Church's mystery: what is quietly happening with God underneath.

how: Diocesan hermits profess the evangelical counsels publicly before their bishop and live in solitude, silence and prayer under his guidance. Consecrated virgins are consecrated by their bishop in a solemn rite and may live in community or in the world, some keeping their ordinary jobs.

games.q: what does “hermits and consecrated virgins” mean?
o: two kinds of nuns who live inside one convent
old callings of solitude, and of lifelong consecration
titles given to saints after they have died

p: a whistling of a gentle air

s: a consecrated virgin must live in a convent
she may live in community, or in the world, at her own job, under the bishop's care.
in Elijah's story, the Lord was in the fire
not the wind, not the earthquake, not the fire, but "a whistling of a gentle air."
Church law recognizes hermits who make vows to their bishop
a diocesan hermit professes the evangelical counsels in the bishop's hands and lives under his guidance.

games.q: you're a woman who has never married. you want to give your whole life to Christ, but you don't feel called to a religious order, and you love your job. what does the Church offer?
o: nothing: give your life to Christ means joining an order.
consecration by your bishop as a consecrated virgin, living in the world.
a private promise that the Church never recognizes.
games.why: an ancient calling the Church still keeps: the bishop consecrates her, and she can keep her job and home under his care.

practice: Somewhere today a hermit is keeping silence, and a woman with a plain ring is at work, and nobody around them knows. Let this quiet be a small share in theirs.
If you pray, ask God to strengthen people whose callings no one sees; if you don't, hold them in mind, unnamed, with good will.

wordCard.voice: Hermits and consecrated virgins. Callings from the Church's early centuries, still lived today: solitude and prayer under a bishop, and lifelong consecration to Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, desert or wilderness: where Elijah fled, and where tradition says the early hermits went to pray.

carryVoice: Your line: ancient callings. Still lived today, mostly where no one is looking. I'll be here tomorrow.
